metaData.originalTitle: LinkedIn Ads CPC benchmarks: How costs compare with Google Ads
metaData.title: LinkedIn Ads CPC benchmarks: How costs compare with Google Ads
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article analyzes $700k+ in LinkedIn Ads spend to provide CPC benchmarks across objectives and industries, compares them with Google Ads, and offers budget and channel mix recommendations for B2B marketers.
metaData.summary: Based on an analysis of over $700,000 in LinkedIn Ads spend (63,000+ clicks, 8.1 million impressions) and corresponding Google Ads data from the same B2B SaaS and professional services clients, the article delivers granular CPC benchmarks. It finds that while LinkedIn's blended average CPC ($11.12) is roughly double Google's ($5.45), the gap narrows significantly when comparing high-intent, cold audiences: non-branded Google Search averages $12.48 versus $13.94 for LinkedIn prospecting campaigns. The author breaks down LinkedIn CPCs by ad objective (ranging from $4.45 for engagement to $71.43 for video views) and by industry (B2B SaaS ~$11.02, professional services ~$15.25), then provides a budget framework ($3k–$5k minimum viable, $5k–$10k testing, $10k+ scaling) and recommends using Google/Microsoft Ads for intent capture and LinkedIn for audience-led demand generation. The article concludes that LinkedIn's higher raw CPC is often justified by access to specific professional audiences and earlier-stage influence in B2B buying cycles.

mainPoints.point: LinkedIn's blended average CPC ($11.12) is roughly double Google's ($5.45), but the gap nearly vanishes for cold, high-intent B2B audiences.
mainPoints.explanation: When comparing non-branded Google Search ($12.48) with LinkedIn prospecting campaigns for lead generation or website conversions ($13.94), the CPC difference is only about 12%, making LinkedIn far more competitive than raw averages suggest.

mainPoints.point: LinkedIn CPCs vary dramatically by ad objective, from $4.45 (engagement) to $71.43 (video views), requiring objective-specific budget planning.
mainPoints.explanation: Lead gen campaigns ($31.29 CPC) are expensive but often justified by higher conversion rates and lead quality; video view CPC is misleading because CPV is the relevant metric. Website visit campaigns average $6.75, a more cost-effective option for traffic generation.

mainPoints.point: Industry matters: B2B SaaS sees lower CPCs (~$11 average) than professional services (~$15), but sample sizes differ.
mainPoints.explanation: B2B SaaS had a larger and more diverse campaign mix, likely lowering its blended CPC. Professional services campaigns used very specific targeting, which can drive up CPCs. Lead gen CPCs for professional services were actually lower than for B2B SaaS, a notable exception.

mainPoints.point: A practical budget framework: $3k–$5k/month minimum viable, $5k–$10k for testing, $10k+ for scaling with full-funnel campaigns.
mainPoints.explanation: Below $3k, meaningful lead volume is unlikely. For B2B companies with an ACV above $20k, starting at $5k/month is recommended. At scale, you can run brand awareness alongside direct response campaigns, including retargeting and list-based targeting.

mainPoints.point: The optimal channel mix: Google Ads for intent capture (branded/non-branded search, remarketing) and LinkedIn for audience-led demand generation, run in parallel.
mainPoints.explanation: Google captures existing demand from active researchers; LinkedIn creates new demand by reaching exact buyer personas early in the decision process. Combined, they form a complementary strategy that covers the full B2B funnel.

keyQuotes: LinkedIn is more expensive than Google on a raw CPC basis, but when you compare apples to apples (both platforms reaching cold, qualified B2B buyers), the gap narrows significantly.
My take is to use LinkedIn Ads to build intent and tell your story, and use Google Ads and Microsoft Ads to capture intent.
The ideal scenario is for your brand to become an active participant in the decision-making process, shaping the narrative instead of letting competitors do it for you.
